newsitem.title: FRANCE: Euro-court hears case of fired Falklands veteran.
newsitem.headline: Euro-court hears case of fired Falklands veteran.

text.p: The European Court of Human Rights on Wednesday heard the case of a British veteran of the Falklands war who was dismissed from the army and jailed for two years after holding fellow-soldiers at gunppoint.

Alex Findlay, 35, submitted his case to the Strasbourg-based European Commission of Human Rights in 1993, arguing that the 1991 court-martial sentencing him to jail and subsequent reviews of the case were unfair, and those who sentenced him were neither independent nor impartial.

In July 1990, after a heavy bout of drinking while on duty in Northern Ireland, Findlay held members of his unit at gunpoint and threatened to kill them and himself. After firing two shots which injured no one, he surrendered and was arrested.
Psychiatric reports indicated that he had suffered post-traumatic stress disorder resulting from his experience during the 1982 Falklands Islands war with Argentina.
A corporal in the Scots Guards, he witnessed horrific scenes in the fight for Mount Tumbledown, one of the fiercest battles of the short war.
Findlay's lawyer has said that Britain had failed to develop treatment for post-traumatic stress disorder although it was recognised by many other countries.
In 1994, British authorities awarded Findlay 100,000 pounds ($156,000) in an out-of-court settlement as compensation for post-battle trauma.
In September of last year, the Commission found that Britain had violated Findlay's right to a fair trial, and passed his case on to the Court.
The Court is expected to rule in six months to a year. The Commission has no binding legal authority but the Court usually follows its advice.
